question: Nine athletes, no two of whom are the same height, try out for the basketball team. One at a time, they draw a wristband at random, without replacement, from a bag containing \(3\) blue bands, \(3\) red bands, and \(3\) green bands. They are divided into a blue group, a red group, and a green group. The tallest member of each group is named the group captain. What is the probability that the group captains are the three tallest athletes?
solution:
The three tallest athletes are all captains exactly when they receive three different colors. If two receive the same color, the shorter of those two cannot be captain. If all three receive different colors, each is taller than everyone else in their group.

Random drawing assigns the nine individual bands uniformly to the athletes. Thus we may calculate as though the three tallest draw first, since changing the drawing order does not favor any assignment.

The tallest athlete may draw any color. Of the eight bands remaining, six have a different color, so the second tallest draws a different color with probability \(6/8\).

Provided those two colors differ, all three bands of the unused color remain among the seven remaining bands. The third tallest therefore completes the required three colors with probability \(3/7\).

Multiplying these successive probabilities gives
\[
\frac{6}{8}\cdot\frac{3}{7}=\boxed{\frac{9}{28}}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\mathrm{C}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
We only need to know which three bands reach the three tallest athletes, so we can count unordered sets of bands.

Temporarily label the nine bands so that even bands of the same color are distinguishable. Every three-band set is equally likely to reach these athletes: each set has the same number of assignments to them and the remaining athletes. There are
\[
\binom{9}{3}=\frac{9\cdot8\cdot7}{3\cdot2\cdot1}=84
\]
such sets. Dividing by \(3\cdot2\cdot1\) removes the six orders in which each set could be listed.

The three tallest athletes are all captains precisely when their bands have different colors. Sharing a color prevents the shorter athlete from being captain, while having different colors makes each the tallest in their group.

A favorable set contains one blue, one red, and one green band. There are three choices for each color, giving \(3\cdot3\cdot3=27\) favorable sets. Every favorable set is counted once because its colors identify the three selections.

Therefore the probability is
\[
\frac{27}{84}=\boxed{\frac{9}{28}},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
